3.1

Parity and the intermediate value theorem

The number of roots on each half line has a definite parity, determined by the boundary value of P (or equivalently of f ) and the end behavior:

Proposition 6 (Exterior root detection). Let d ≥ 2.

(i) On (u, ∞): since P (t) → +∞ as t → +∞, the number of roots is odd if P (u) < 0 (i.e., f (0) < 0) and even if P (u) ≥ 0 (i.e., f (0) ≥ 0).

(ii) On (−∞, −u): since P (t) → (−1)d · ∞ as t → −∞, the parity depends on both P (−u) and the degree. Specifically:

• If d is even: the number of roots is odd if P (−u) < 0 (i.e., f (π) < 0) and even if P (−u) ≥ 0.

• If d is odd: the number of roots is odd if P (−u) > 0 (i.e., f (π) > 0) and even if P (−u) ≤ 0.

In the generic case (at most one root per half line), the exterior root count is:

4 Critical point analysis

To count the zeros of f on [0, π], we study its critical points. Differentiating (5) and factoring out sin θ > 0 on (0, π):

Proposition 7. The interior critical points of f in (0, π) are the solutions of a polynomial equation of degree d − 1 in x = cos θ. Consequently, f has at most d − 1 interior critical points, and therefore at most d zeros in [0, π] consistent with P having at most d real roots.
